Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We investigate the large baryon number sector of the Einstein-Skyrme model as a possible model for baryon stars. Gravitating hedgehog skyrmions have been investigated previously and the existence of stable solitonic stars excluded due to energy considerations. However, in this paper we demonstrate that by generating gravitating skyrmions using rational maps, we can achieve multi-baryon bound states whilst recovering spherical symmetry in the limit where B becomes large.

Gravitating hedgehog Skyrmions have been studied previously, and the existence of stable solitonic stars has been ruled out on energetic grounds. However, in this paper we demonstrate that, by constructing gravitating Skyrmions using rational maps, one can obtain multi-baryon bound states while recovering spherical symmetry in the limit of large \(B\).
outputs.L2: We examine whether the high-baryon-number regime of the Einstein–Skyrme model can serve as a description of baryon stars. Earlier studies considered gravitating hedgehog skyrmions and ruled out stable soliton-like stellar configurations on energetic grounds. In contrast, we show here that constructing gravitating skyrmions through rational maps permits the formation of bound states with multiple baryons, while spherical symmetry is restored as the baryon number \(B\) becomes large.

The text examines the large-baryon-number sector of the Einstein–Skyrme model as a possible framework for describing baryon stars. In this context, baryon stars are understood as compact, self-gravitating configurations made from Skyrme matter, where the conserved baryon number of the Skyrme field plays the role of the total number of baryons. The central question is whether gravity can support stable, solitonic objects carrying very large baryon number.

Earlier investigations focused mainly on gravitating hedgehog skyrmions. In the hedgehog ansatz, the Skyrme field is constrained to have a highly symmetric form, and this makes the field equations more tractable. However, studies based on this ansatz concluded that stable solitonic stars were unlikely to exist. The main reason was energetic: the resulting configurations did not exhibit the necessary binding properties. In particular, their energies did not suggest that large multi-baryon objects could be stable against decay into smaller constituents or individual baryons.

The paper revisits this issue using a broader class of Skyrme-field configurations generated by rational maps. Rational maps are known to provide good approximations to multi-skyrmion solutions in flat space, especially for configurations with baryon number greater than one. By incorporating rational-map skyrmions into the Einstein–Skyrme model, the authors show that gravity can support multi-baryon bound states. These solutions have lower energy per baryon than the corresponding collection of isolated single-baryon configurations, indicating that genuine gravitationally bound multi-skyrmion states can exist.

A key advantage of the rational map approach is that it captures the angular structure of multi-skyrmions while reducing the problem to a more manageable radial form. Although finite-baryon-number rational-map configurations are generally not exactly spherically symmetric, their angular energy distributions become increasingly uniform as the baryon number grows. As a result, spherical symmetry is effectively recovered in the large-baryon-number limit. This makes the rational map ansatz especially useful for studying baryon-star-like configurations, where one expects the matter distribution to become approximately spherical at macroscopic scales.

Overall, the text argues that earlier negative conclusions based on the hedgehog ansatz were too restrictive. By using rational maps, the Einstein–Skyrme model admits large multi-baryon configurations with binding properties more consistent with the idea of stable baryon stars.

The Einstein-Skyrme model provides a natural framework for studying compact objects made from baryonic solitons. In this model, baryons are described not as point particles or as a fluid, but as topological solitons of a nonlinear meson field, while gravity is incorporated through coupling to the Einstein equations. This makes the model an interesting candidate for describing hypothetical baryon stars: self-gravitating objects whose stability is supported by the topological structure of the Skyrme field rather than by conventional matter pressure alone.

Previous studies of gravitating skyrmions often focused on the simplest configuration, the spherically symmetric hedgehog ansatz. This ansatz describes a single baryon number configuration very effectively, but it is too restrictive for studying systems with large baryon number. In flat space, multi-skyrmions are known to possess rich, often highly non-spherical structures, and their angular dependence is well captured by the rational map ansatz. The rational map approach separates the radial profile of the Skyrme field from its angular structure, allowing one to construct approximate multi-skyrmion configurations with arbitrary baryon number while retaining much of the essential topology and geometry of the exact solutions.

The text therefore investigates the large-baryon-number sector of the Einstein-Skyrme model using rational maps rather than relying solely on the hedgehog ansatz. By coupling rational-map skyrmions to gravity, one can explore how multi-baryon soliton configurations behave when their own gravitational field becomes important. This is especially relevant for the question of whether the Skyrme model can support stable, star-like objects composed of many baryons.

A central result is that gravitating rational-map skyrmions can form bound states with baryon number greater than one. In other words, the energy per baryon of certain multi-skyrmion configurations can be lower than that of isolated single-baryon configurations, indicating that the solitons prefer to bind together. Gravity strengthens this tendency by providing an additional attractive interaction, while the Skyrme term and the topology of the field prevent collapse. The competition between these effects produces stable self-gravitating soliton configurations over a range of parameters.

The use of rational maps also reveals how the geometry of multi-skyrmions changes as the baryon number increases. For small baryon numbers, the configurations may retain the discrete symmetries familiar from flat-space Skyrmions, such as tetrahedral, cubic, or other polyhedral structures. However, as the baryon number becomes large, the angular distribution becomes increasingly uniform. In this limit, the rational-map configurations approach spherical symmetry, making them resemble macroscopic compact objects more closely than small, individual skyrmions.

This recovery of approximate spherical symmetry at large baryon number is important for the interpretation of these solutions as baryon-star models. A realistic star is expected to be nearly spherical when isolated and non-rotating, and the rational-map construction shows that such symmetry can emerge naturally from many-baryon soliton configurations, even though the underlying finite-baryon-number solutions may be non-spherical. Thus, the rational map ansatz bridges the gap between microscopic Skyrmion structure and macroscopic stellar behavior.

The analysis suggests that the Einstein-Skyrme model has a viable large-baryon-number sector capable of supporting stable, self-gravitating solitonic matter. Rational-map gravitating skyrmions provide a more flexible and physically relevant description than the hedgehog ansatz alone, because they allow multi-baryon configurations and capture the binding and symmetry properties expected of large Skyrmion systems. These results point toward a possible solitonic model of baryon stars, in which the star is understood as a large, gravitationally bound Skyrmion carrying a high topological charge.

Overall, the text argues that rational maps are a powerful tool for extending the study of the Einstein-Skyrme model beyond the single-baryon sector. They make it possible to construct and analyze gravitating multi-skyrmions, demonstrate the existence of multi-baryon bound states, and show how spherical symmetry can re-emerge in the large-baryon-number limit. This supports the idea that stable baryon-star configurations may exist within the Einstein-Skyrme theory and motivates further investigation of their masses, radii, stability ranges, and possible astrophysical relevance.

The **Einstein–Skyrme model** describes a class of **gravitating Skyrmions**, where the nonlinear field theory introduced by Tony Skyrme is coupled to Einstein’s theory of general relativity. In the original Skyrme model, baryons are represented as topological solitons of a pion field. These solitons are stable because of a conserved topological charge, which is interpreted as baryon number.

When gravity is included, the system becomes richer and more complex. The Skyrme field contributes energy and pressure, which curve spacetime according to the **Einstein field equations**. At the same time, the curved geometry affects the structure and stability of the Skyrmion. This mutual interaction leads to solutions known as **gravitating Skyrmions**.

A central question in the Einstein–Skyrme theory is how strong gravity modifies the properties of solitons. For weak gravitational coupling, gravitating Skyrmions resemble their flat-space counterparts. As the strength of gravity increases, their size, mass, and stability can change significantly. In some cases, the solutions may approach black hole configurations, leading to objects sometimes called **Skyrme black holes**, where a black hole is surrounded by nontrivial Skyrme field structure.

The Einstein–Skyrme system is important because it connects several areas of theoretical physics: general relativity, nonlinear field theory, topology, and nuclear physics. It provides a useful model for studying how topological matter behaves under gravitational interaction, and it also offers insights into possible exotic compact objects in the universe.

In summary, the study of **Einstein–Skyrme gravitating systems** explores how Skyrmions behave when their energy and topology are allowed to influence spacetime. These models show that gravity can dramatically affect soliton solutions, making them a valuable subject in mathematical physics and gravitational theory.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a concise abstract for a theoretical physics paper on large baryon number Einstein-Skyrme models, baryon stars, and rational map gravitating skyrmions.
counterfactuals.output: We investigate large baryon number solutions of the Einstein–Skyrme model as effective descriptions of self-gravitating baryonic matter. Using the rational map ansatz, we reduce the gravitating Skyrme field equations to a tractable radial system while retaining the topological structure associated with high-degree maps. We analyze the dependence of mass, radius, binding energy, and compactness on baryon number and gravitational coupling, identifying regimes in which multi-Skyrmion configurations approach macroscopic “baryon star” behavior. The solutions exhibit the characteristic branch structure of gravitating solitons, with stable weak-gravity configurations connected to strongly gravitating branches near critical coupling. Our results clarify how topological charge, Skyrme repulsion, and gravitational attraction compete in the large-\(B\) limit, providing a bridge between finite baryon-number Skyrmions and compact astrophysical objects modeled within a fully relativistic field theory.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a research article arguing that rational maps allow stable multi-baryon bound states in the Einstein-Skyrme model, unlike earlier hedgehog skyrmion approaches.
counterfactuals.output:
The article argues that **rational map Skyrmions provide a much better description of gravitating multi-baryon states in the Einstein–Skyrme model** than earlier spherically symmetric “hedgehog” constructions.

In the Einstein–Skyrme model, baryons are modeled as topological solitons of a nonlinear pion field coupled to gravity. Earlier studies often used the **hedgehog ansatz**, which is natural for baryon number \(B=1\) because it imposes spherical symmetry. However, for \(B>1\), true Skyrmions are generally **not spherically symmetric**. Forcing a multi-baryon configuration into a hedgehog form artificially raises its energy and can make multi-baryon bound states appear unstable or only weakly bound.

The article instead uses the **rational map ansatz**, where the Skyrme field is decomposed into:

- a radial profile function, and  
- an angular dependence described by a rational map between Riemann spheres.

This construction captures the correct polyhedral symmetries of flat-space multi-Skyrmions, such as toroidal, tetrahedral, cubic, or icosahedral structures, depending on baryon number. It therefore gives a much more realistic approximation to multi-baryon configurations.

When coupled to gravity, the rational map approach shows that **stable bound states with baryon number \(B>1\)** can exist. The gravitational field lowers the total energy and supports configurations where the mass per baryon is less than that of isolated \(B=1\) Skyrmions. Thus, the multi-baryon systems are genuinely bound.

A central point of the article is that the apparent failure of earlier hedgehog-based studies to find stable multi-baryon bound states was largely due to the overly restrictive ansatz. The hedgehog ansatz forces all baryon number into a spherically symmetric configuration, which is not energetically optimal for \(B>1\). Rational maps allow the field to distribute baryon density in angularly structured ways, reducing the energy and producing stable solutions.

The paper likely analyzes how the solutions depend on the gravitational coupling. As in many Einstein–Skyrme systems, one typically finds branches of gravitating Skyrmions: a branch connected to the flat-space Skyrmion at weak gravity and another branch that may approach a limiting or unstable configuration at stronger coupling. The rational map ansatz allows these branches to be studied for higher baryon numbers while preserving the essential non-spherical structure of the Skyrme field.

Overall, the article’s main conclusion is that **multi-baryon bound states are compatible with the Einstein–Skyrme model once the correct Skyrmion geometry is included**. Rational maps overcome the limitations of the hedgehog approximation and demonstrate that gravity can stabilize or enhance binding among multi-Skyrmion configurations.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.output: Gravitating skyrmions provide a natural effective-field-theoretic framework for modeling compact objects whose matter content is fundamentally baryonic, since the topological charge \(B\) of the Skyrme field is identified with baryon number. In this setting, “baryon stars” may be described as self-gravitating configurations of large baryon number, obtained by coupling the Skyrme model to general relativity and studying finite-energy solutions of the resulting Einstein–Skyrme equations. While low-\(B\) skyrmions are typically highly structured and possess only discrete spatial symmetries, the large-\(B\) regime is expected to smooth out microscopic shell-like and crystalline features, leading to an effective macroscopic description in which spherical symmetry is recovered to a good approximation. This recovery is essential for connecting the topological soliton picture to conventional relativistic stellar models, where equilibrium configurations are often described by spherically symmetric metrics and radial matter profiles. Thus, the large-\(B\) limit of gravitating skyrmions offers a bridge between microscopic baryonic soliton dynamics and phenomenological models of dense compact stars, while retaining a direct link between stellar mass, geometry, and conserved baryon number.

counterfactuals.prompt: In formal physics prose, describe how rational map ansätze improve on hedgehog skyrmions in the Einstein-Skyrme model by producing bound multi-baryon configurations at large baryon number.
counterfactuals.output:
In the Einstein–Skyrme model, the spherically symmetric hedgehog ansatz provides a natural description of the unit-baryon sector, and, in a gravitational setting, of its corresponding self-gravitating generalizations. Its usefulness becomes much more limited for baryon number \(B>1\). A simple higher-charge hedgehog configuration is typically too symmetric and too energetically costly: it effectively forces the angular structure of a multi-skyrmion into a spherical form that does not capture the known tendency of Skyrme solitons to form spatially structured, shell-like or polyhedral configurations. As a result, hedgehog-type multi-baryon fields generally do not give good approximations to bound multi-skyrmions.

The rational map ansatz improves this situation by separating the Skyrme field into a radial profile and a nontrivial angular map. One writes the chiral field schematically as  
\[
U(r,z)=\exp\!\left[i f(r)\,\hat{\mathbf n}_{R(z)}\cdot \boldsymbol{\tau}\right],
\]
where \(f(r)\) is a radial profile function, \(z\) is a stereographic coordinate on the two-sphere, and \(R(z)\) is a rational map between Riemann spheres. The degree of \(R\) is identified with the baryon number \(B\). Thus the baryon charge is encoded not by imposing a higher winding hedgehog, but by allowing a nontrivial angular distribution determined by the rational map.

This construction is especially effective at large baryon number because it captures the angular organization of multi-skyrmions while retaining a tractable one-dimensional radial variational problem. The rational map can be chosen to minimize an angular functional, and the remaining profile equation determines the radial size and shape of the soliton. In flat space this yields accurate approximations to polyhedral multi-skyrmions; in the Einstein–Skyrme model it similarly provides a controlled way to construct self-gravitating multi-baryon configurations.

The essential improvement is that the rational map ansatz allows the energy density and baryon density to distribute themselves over a non-spherical angular pattern, rather than being constrained to the hedgehog form. This lowers the energy per baryon relative to naive spherically symmetric multi-winding configurations and permits the formation of genuinely bound states with \(B>1\). In the gravitational theory, the same mechanism persists, with gravity further modifying the radial profile and possibly enhancing binding in certain parameter regimes.

Consequently, rational map ansätze supply a physically meaningful approximation to large-\(B\) Einstein–Skyrme solitons: they preserve the topological charge, incorporate the angular structure required for binding, and reduce the full coupled Einstein–Skyrme equations to a more manageable variational problem. They therefore constitute a substantial improvement over hedgehog skyrmions for describing bound multi-baryon configurations at high baryon number.
